interviewQuestions.question: One key is getting 100x the traffic of others — how do you handle it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd first rule out the obvious wrong fix: adding more cache nodes doesn't help here, because this specific key still lives on one node regardless of how many others exist in the cluster — new nodes take on other keys, not a share of this one.

I'd propose two concrete fixes depending on the shape of the traffic. If it's mostly reads, I'd cache the key locally, in-process, on every app node, in front of the distributed cache — most reads get absorbed before they ever reach the cluster. If local caching alone isn't enough, or the key genuinely needs to live in the shared cache, I'd shard it into N physical keys spread across different nodes by the cluster's normal hashing, with reads picking one or merging across all N.

I'd also ask a clarifying question up front — is this a celebrity user, a viral post, or a misbehaving client retrying — since a client bug might need rate-limiting instead of any caching change at all.

**Testing:** whether you know a single key can't be trivially sharded by adding nodes, and have a fix that actually operates on that key.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fixing a single overloaded key

interviewQuestions.question: How would you detect a hot key before it takes down a node, rather than finding out from an outage?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd build two layers of detection rather than relying on an incident to tell me. First, per-key traffic sampling at the cache client or proxy layer, tracking the top-N most-requested keys in a rolling window — this directly surfaces a key trending toward hot before it becomes catastrophic. Second, per-node load monitoring that alerts when one node's traffic is disproportionate to its peers, which is often visible even before you've identified the specific key responsible.

I'd tie the two together: a node-load alert tells you *something* is wrong right now, and the per-key sampling tells you *which key* to act on. Catching this early means you can apply local caching or key splitting proactively, on your own timeline, instead of scrambling during an active incident.

I'd also mention this pairs naturally with the celebrity/viral/client-bug diagnosis — the sampling data itself often reveals which of those three you're dealing with.

**Testing:** whether detection is part of your design, not something you only think about after a postmortem.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Follow-up: detecting a hot key proactively

interviewQuestions.question: The hot key is also being written to frequently, not just read — does your fix still work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd be upfront that this makes the problem meaningfully harder. Local caching still helps the read side, but frequent writes mean each node's local copy needs frequent invalidation to stay correct, eating into the benefit it was supposed to provide.

Key splitting gets worse in a specific way: every write now has to fan out to all N physical keys to keep them consistent with each other, so a key that's both hot-read and hot-write turns N-way splitting into N times the write cost — not a free lunch the way it looked for a mostly-read celebrity profile.

So I'd shift the approach: instead of purely scaling reads, I'd look at reducing write frequency itself — batching updates instead of writing on every event, or accepting slightly looser consistency (an approximate counter instead of an exact one) if the product can tolerate it. I'd frame this as the point where the problem stops being purely a caching-layer fix and starts requiring a change to the write pattern itself.

**Testing:** whether you recognize the read-focused fixes don't fully carry over, instead of assuming the same toolkit just works.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Follow-up: a hot key that's also hot-write
